title: Artificial intelligence (AI) and other new technology in the workplace, including monitoring and surveillance — UNISON bargaining guide (September 2025 edition)
pub: UNISON — the public service union (branch bargaining guide, 'Last updated September 2025')
author: UNISON

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source addresses workplace surveillance, privacy and employee agreement rather than the implementation, verification or task-specific evaluation of AI-enabled legal services. Its governance concerns are broadly analogous, but it does not provide enough evidence to establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: UNISON accepts the cluster’s core view that AI primarily changes tasks, with benefits depending on selective, human-centred implementation rather than wholesale replacement. It materially extends the proposition by specifying worker-centred operating-model and governance mechanisms: early collective consultation, lifecycle involvement, meaningful human oversight, recurring impact assessment, training, job-quality protections and fair distribution of productivity gains.
qs: Most roles will be changed rather than eliminated entirely, with technology taking over some tasks while humans focus on others.
Ideally the union is involved in   discussions early in considerations when new technology is to be introduced - in   the design, procurement, trial, implementation, review and maintenance.

st.t: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation
st.an: UNISON accepts the cluster’s contingent account: workplace outcomes depend heavily on implementation, worker influence and organisational choices. It materially develops that proposition by specifying lifecycle consultation, transparency, human review, impact assessment, bargaining resources and transition protections, while presenting these mainly as proposed safeguards rather than proof that consultation guarantees benefits.
qs: Whether this positive vision is realised depends greatly on how the technology is to be implemented.
Ideally the union is involved in   discussions early in considerations when new technology is to be introduced - in   the design, procurement, trial, implementation, review and maintenance.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: UNISON supports the cluster’s core framing: AI more often augments workers and reallocates tasks than replaces whole roles, while benefits depend on implementation and can be offset by deskilling and other workplace harms. Its evidence is cross-sector rather than legal-specific, so it reinforces the proposition without directly establishing legal competence or apprenticeship effects.
qs: More common is augmentation, where technology works alongside humans, supporting them in their tasks rather than replacing them entirely.

    Constant performance monitoring through digital systems can create          significant stress          Some workers may find their roles deskilled as tasks are simplified or          automated.

kp.k: Worker-centred augmentation is UNISON’s preferred model
kp.d: UNISON argues that AI can remove repetitive tasks, improve accessibility and safety, and improve public services, but that implementation must protect workers and service users against displacement, discrimination, surveillance and work intensification. Its position is a bargaining and policy recommendation, not a finding that these benefits necessarily occur.
qs: AI should be used to augment and support workers, not replace or control them
The benefits from increased productivity through AI should be shared with workers.

kp.k: Public-sector fiscal pressures can distort technology adoption
kp.d: The guide describes AI as already changing public services and notes the government’s pledge of over £2 billion for NHS technology and digital transformation in the 2024 autumn budget. UNISON warns that budget-driven adoption may prioritise staffing cuts over demonstrated service improvements, with implications for citizens as well as employees.
qs: However, UNISON is concerned that this approach may prioritise cost-cutting over genuine service improvement.
AI solutions may be introduced to the public sector without sufficient assessment of their risks or evidence of their effectiveness.

kp.k: Adoption statistics and productivity forecasts measure different things
kp.d: The guide reports a 2023 Pissarides Review study finding around 80% of UK firms had adopted AI, robotic or automated equipment in the preceding three years—not AI alone. Separately, it attributes to KPMG’s June 2023 report a forecast that generative AI could increase UK productivity by 1.2%, equivalent to £31 billion annually at 2022 GDP levels, with 40% of jobs seeing some impact. These are reported forecasts rather than realised gains.
qs: Overall, they estimate that 40% of jobs are expected to see some impact from the technology.
Employers expect new technology to increase their productivity and profits.

kp.k: Task transformation is more common than complete job automation
kp.d: The guide distinguishes automation that replaces tasks from augmentation that supports human workers. Although it reports IPPR’s estimate that up to 8 million UK jobs could be at risk, it qualifies displacement predictions by arguing that most roles will change rather than disappear. It cites healthcare as an augmentation example, with clinicians retaining final decisions and care delivery, and notes that newly created jobs may require different skills.
qs: However, complete automation of entire jobs is relatively rare.
Most roles will be changed rather than eliminated entirely, with technology taking over some tasks while humans focus on others.
Whether this positive vision is realised depends greatly on how the technology is to be implemented.

kp.k: Entry-level exposure raises distributional and employment concerns
kp.d: UNISON identifies back-office, entry-level and part-time work as potentially highly exposed, with women, young people and Black workers overrepresented in susceptible roles. It reports the August 2025 Stanford paper’s finding of a 13% relative employment decline among US workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations since widespread generative AI adoption, with declines concentrated in automation-oriented occupations. This is a reported cross-domain labour-market finding, not evidence about junior lawyers specifically.
qs: Studies consistently show that low-paid jobs are much more likely to include tasks that can be automated, with back office, entry-level, and part-time roles potentially facing the greatest exposure.
Furthermore, employment declines are concentrated in occupations where AI is more likely to automate, rather than augment, human labour.

kp.k: Council example contrasts augmentation assurances with eliminated positions
kp.d: The guide reports Derby City Council’s February 2024 announcement of a £7 million AI development contract and copilots in three service areas, presented as freeing staff for higher-value work. It contrasts those assurances with a subsequent FOI disclosure of two eliminated full-time-equivalent customer management positions; this is a local example rather than an aggregate displacement estimate.
qs: Despite denial of claims it would lead to job losses, a recent FOI request disclosed that two full-time equivalent positions in the customer management department had been eliminated.

kp.k: Administrative support offers substantial but conditional time savings
kp.d: The guide reports that a 2023 survey of UK public-service professionals found 45% aware of generative AI use in their work area and 22% actively using it. It attributes to a June 2025 Alan Turing Institute study an estimate that around 40% of public-sector time could be supported by generative AI. Workers reportedly spend an average of 30 minutes daily on email, with initial drafting support potentially reducing that time by 70%; supportable time is not equated with eliminated jobs.
qs: According to the Alan Turing Institute in their June 2025 study, around 40% of public sector time could be supported by generative AI, being particularly useful for roles that have high levels of administrative tasks.
Similarly, almost all time spent creating or updating records, databases, case files and documents could be supported.

kp.k: Algorithmic management extends control across the employment lifecycle
kp.d: The guide describes systems allocating shifts and tasks, monitoring productivity, managing absence, triggering discipline and terminating access to work. It warns that apparently neutral metrics can intensify work and feed unrealistic expectations into performance-related pay. Citing ITUC research on US nursing platforms, it also reports lower-pay pressures, scheduling uncertainty, weak safety accountability and unfamiliar clinical placements without onboarding.
qs: The performance of workers may be tracked against unrealistic expectations that then feed into performance-related pay systems.
Unsurprisingly, as a consequence service delivery may also be affected detrimentally.

kp.k: Automating easy work can intensify remaining human tasks
kp.d: Drawing on UNISON’s 2025 energy seminar, the guide describes call-centre chatbots and automated triage removing simpler queries while leaving staff with difficult interactions. It argues that employers are not adequately accounting for increased abuse and longer calls. More generally, it identifies risks of reduced autonomy, deskilling, escalating targets and cognitive overload alongside possible efficiency benefits.
qs: Increasingly this means that workers are becoming responsible for only the most complex or difficult calls.
Yet the implications of this – more abuse from customers, more time taken on calls etc – are not being taken into consideration by employers.

kp.k: Wellbeing evidence is mixed and context-dependent
kp.d: The guide reports Institute for the Future of Work research associating conventional ICT exposure with higher quality of life and newer technologies such as wearables, robotics and AI with lower quality of life; these are correlations. Its account of a 2025 qualitative study specifies 12 focus groups and 84 participants across sectors and occupational levels, finding mixed effects on flexibility, autonomy, skills, meaningfulness and work-life balance.
qs: Frequent exposure to these technologies was correlated with lower life quality scores for most respondents.
This negative correlation was particularly evident among women aged 35-49.
Some workers report increased work intensity and blurred work-life boundaries, while others experience benefits in these areas.

kp.k: Surveillance can undermine privacy, trust and union representation
kp.d: The guide describes keystroke logging, webcams, location tracking, biometric attendance checks and communication analysis expanding managerial visibility, including into homes. It reports September 2025 Guardian coverage of CMI research finding a third of employers using bossware, with a similar proportion unaware of their organisation’s tracking. It also relays the TUC’s warning that AI might profile union activity and argues excessive monitoring may damage trust, retention and service delivery.
qs: Overuse of monitoring and surveillance tools can erode the relationship of mutual trust and confidence that should exist between workers and their employer.
Monitoring communications between a worker and their union representative or capturing a worker’s personal correspondence both give rise to significant concerns.

kp.k: Opaque systems impede challenges to discriminatory decisions
kp.d: UNISON argues that historical bias and human design choices can produce discriminatory outcomes in recruitment, performance management and service allocation. Vendor ownership and black-box operation may leave even employers unable to explain decisions. The guide also distinguishes plausible but fabricated generative outputs from reliable information, warning that errors and bias have especially serious consequences for vulnerable public-service users.
qs: Human choices about how to build and use data-driven technologies are never neutral.
When AI makes or assists with decisions that affect service users, particularly vulnerable individuals, any errors or biases can have serious consequences.
For example, flawed algorithmic assessments of needs could lead to inappropriate care packages or resource allocation.

kp.k: Clinical summarisation illustrates unequal treatment within administrative automation
kp.d: The guide reports a 2025 NIHR study of LLM-generated long-term-care case notes: some models emphasised men’s physical and mental health more strongly and downplayed women’s needs. The study is presented as supporting bias evaluation despite potential administrative benefits, with unequal service receipt identified as a possible downstream consequence rather than an established outcome.
qs: Language used for men was more direct, with women’s needs downplayed more often than men’s.
In this particular usage, if women’s health issues are underemphasised, this may lead to gender-based disparities in service receipt.

kp.k: Recruitment audits reveal discrimination and excessive data collection
kp.d: The guide cites the ICO’s 2024 recruitment-tool audit finding protected-characteristic filtering, inferred demographic data insufficiently accurate for bias monitoring, processing without lawful basis or candidate knowledge, and excessive scraping. Separately, University of Sussex research on asynchronous video interviews is reported as finding discomfort, uncertainty about assessment and emotional and cognitive exhaustion; asynchronous interviews are not treated as necessarily AI-led.
qs: features in some tools could lead to discrimination by having a search functionality that allowed recruiters to filter out candidates with certain protected characteristics.
It was often processed without a lawful basis and without the candidate’s knowledge.
Recruiters and candidates were rarely aware that information was being repurposed in this way.

kp.k: Employers remain accountable despite delegation to AI vendors
kp.d: The guide maintains that employers retain responsibility for fairness, dismissal, equality, health and safety, privacy and contractual obligations when using AI. It calls unclear responsibility between employers, users and third-party developers 'managerial fuzz'. It also cites EHRC guidance that the Public Sector Equality Duty applies when systems are externally developed, purchased or operated on a public body’s behalf.
qs: The employer remains responsible for decisions made using AI.
Therefore, areas of employer responsibility covered by legislation, including dismissal, health and safety and equality, are not reduced by the use of new technology.

kp.k: Automated-decision law is changing during the guide’s timeframe
kp.d: The guide explains UK GDPR protections concerning significant solely automated decisions, transparency, challenge and human intervention. Its appendix separately notes that the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amends rather than replaces existing legislation, with changes phased between June 2025 and June 2026. It describes a more permissive automated-decision framework retaining safeguards, and a requirement by June 2026 for organisational complaints procedures acknowledging complaints within 30 days.
qs: The changes will be phased in between June 2025 and June 2026.
Organisations will be able to make such decisions in wider circumstances but must implement certain safeguards.

kp.k: UNISON advocates stronger statutory rights beyond existing protections
kp.d: UNISON supports the TUC’s Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment) Bill as a proposal to fill legal gaps. The guide lists consultation duties for high-risk AI, personalised explanations, human review, restrictions on harmful emotion recognition, stronger discrimination protections, protection against AI-based unfair dismissal, greater union data access and a statutory right to disconnect. These are advocated reforms, not described as enacted rights.
qs: Unfortunately, there are still significant gaps in the current legal framework.
Create a statutory right to disconnect from work, allowing workers to switch off outside working hours

kp.k: Collective bargaining should govern the entire technology lifecycle
kp.d: The guide recommends mapping existing systems, collecting worker experiences, documenting ownership and responsibilities, and establishing a joint negotiating committee before proposals are settled. It proposes accessible registers, independent expertise, pilots with success criteria, ongoing review and mechanisms to modify harmful systems. Consultation is intended to cover design and procurement as well as deployment, rather than merely explaining a completed purchase.
qs: Ideally, as part of any collective agreement, the employer will agree to consult reps at each stage of development, procurement, and application of AI and digital or algorithmic management systems (AMS).
A register will be maintained by the employer, explaining how new technology and AI is being used in the workplace, which all workers and job applicants can access.

kp.k: Risk assessment must address suppliers and work quality
kp.d: UNISON recommends equality, health and safety, data protection and algorithmic impact assessments with worker involvement; its model policy adds environmental assessment. It reports Data Protection Network research from 2024 in which 50% of data protection officers and related professionals said AI risks had not been assessed or were unsure, while fewer than 40% of organisations had assessed relevant suppliers. The guide calls for consideration of deskilling, lost expertise, work intensification and continuity after supplier contracts end.
qs: Additionally less than 40% of organisations have conducted any form of risk assessment of relevant suppliers.
This reveals limited oversight of AI in the supply chain.
Systems should be procured or built in a way that minimises any such risks identified.

kp.k: Training and redeployment should precede redundancy
kp.d: UNISON recommends paid retraining, support targeted at lower-paid and entry-level workers, and redeployment before redundancy. It argues that empathy, creativity and complex problem-solving remain important alongside technical competence. Its proposed agreements seek appropriate grading and pay for expanded roles, preferably no compulsory redundancies, and sharing productivity gains through pay, flexibility or reduced hours. The model policy goes further by proposing no AI-driven reductions or demotions of job roles or expansion of insecure contracts.
qs: Paid time for upskilling and retraining, with priority given to redeployment over redundancy when roles change.
If it can be achieved, a no compulsory redundancy agreement is obviously the most preferable arrangement.
The introduction of new technology and AI will not be used to expand the use of insecure contracts such as zero hours contracts, carrying inferior employment rights.

kp.k: Model policies require human review and explicit usage boundaries
kp.d: The model agreement proposes human review of automated decisions and rights for workers and applicants to respond, including in hiring, promotion, performance evaluation and discipline. The guide suggests generative-AI usage policies distinguishing possible permitted tasks such as proofreading from prohibited uses such as grievance outcomes or disciplinary penalties. These are proposed workplace safeguards, not evidence of universal practice or legal requirements.
qs: No automated decisions will be made by new technology without being reviewed by humans.
Human oversight is required for all decisions on hiring, promotion, performance evaluation, and disciplinary actions.
Workers should never be disadvantaged if they breach rules that have not been properly explained.

kp.k: Biometric enforcement demonstrates necessity and proportionality constraints
kp.d: The guide reports February 2024 ICO enforcement notices against Serco Leisure, Serco Jersey and seven associated community leisure trusts concerning biometric attendance monitoring of more than 2,000 employees across 38 facilities. The organisations had not justified biometrics over less intrusive alternatives or proactively offered alternatives. UNISON uses the case to support early consultation, genuine choice, clear lawful bases and special-category processing conditions.
qs: But they failed to show why it was necessary or proportionate to use FRT and fingerprint scanning for this purpose, when there are less intrusive means available such as ID cards or fobs.

Employees had not been proactively offered an alternative to having their faces and fingers scanned to clock in and out of their place of work, and it was presented as a requirement in order to get paid.

kp.k: Monitoring safeguards should prevent purpose drift and intrusive spillovers
kp.d: The guide repeatedly warns that safety or attendance tools may be repurposed for performance management and discipline without context. It recommends less intrusive alternatives, clear purposes, limited access and retention, privacy during breaks and private vehicle use, and work-provided phones rather than compulsory personal-device apps. It also seeks employer support for staff recorded by the public while recognising legitimate personal-use recordings and the domestic exemption from data protection law.
qs: Difficulties particularly arise when the purpose given is for security or health and safety but then the footage is also used for performance management.
There should be a facility for the employee to switch a button on the device to disable the monitoring.
Far better for the employer to make clear in the first place to the general public, that such activity is not to be tolerated in the workplace.

kp.k: AI business cases must include lifecycle and environmental costs
kp.d: The guide argues that purchase costs alone understate implementation, maintenance, computing, security and compliance burdens. Citing government guidance, it recommends considering alternatives and sustainability. It reports estimates of substantial AI energy and water use and cites a greener-technology procurement survey in which 70% of public-sector technology procurement staff did not consider specific environmental factors. Its model policy proposes environmental assessment of new systems and changes.
qs: New technological systems can be very costly to set up, operate and maintain.
Ongoing investment is needed to maintain these systems, update them with new data if required, and ensure their performance remains stable over time.
Too often employers aiming for greener and more sustainable ways of working and service delivery, neglect their consideration of technology choices.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: UNISON presents AI as an existing transformation of public-service delivery and employment: it can support workers and improve services, but can also displace tasks and jobs, intensify work, extend surveillance and reproduce discrimination.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain bargaining guide, not a source making predictions about legal-service markets. Its claims concern public services, utilities and workplace technology more broadly. UNISON says AI already supports recruitment, scheduling, performance monitoring, administration and service delivery, and predicts increasing public-sector prevalence. It argues that most jobs will change rather than disappear completely: routine tasks can be automated, while augmentation leaves people responsible for judgement and care. Potential benefits include more meaningful work, safer and more accessible workplaces, better decisions and improved efficiency. Conversely, UNISON warns that fiscal pressures may make adoption primarily a cost-cutting exercise, producing redundancies and threatening service quality. It says algorithmic management can reduce discretion, deskill roles, impose unrealistic targets and intrude into private life. Call-centre automation is said to leave staff handling disproportionately complex and difficult calls without corresponding employer recognition of the workload or abuse involved. Opaque systems can make employment and service decisions harder to challenge, while biased training data and fabricated outputs can produce unfair recruitment, inaccurate care assessments and discriminatory service allocation. UNISON also argues that AI can impose substantial acquisition, maintenance, computing and environmental costs. Its preferred response—augmentation, human oversight, worker consultation, retraining and sharing productivity gains—is a bargaining position, not a finding that these protections already operate.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The guide combines secondary research and projections, regulatory findings, workplace cases, worker surveys and union experience; these provide different kinds of support and are not interchangeable.
pts.d: For adoption, UNISON cites a 2023 Pissarides Review study reporting that around 80% of UK firms had adopted AI, robotics or automated equipment during the preceding three years; that figure is not AI-only adoption. A 2023 public-service survey reported 45% awareness of generative-AI use and 22% active use among respondents. For potential productivity, the guide cites KPMG's June 2023 estimate of a 1.2% increase in UK productivity, equivalent to £31 billion annually at 2022 GDP levels, with some impact on 40% of jobs. Here KPMG is the cited research source, not a legal-services entrant. It cites an Alan Turing Institute June 2025 study estimating that generative AI could support around 40% of public-sector working time and reduce time spent on initial email drafting by 70%. These are potential task-support estimates, not demonstrated equivalent headcount reductions. For displacement, it cites IPPR's projection that up to eight million UK jobs could be at risk and Goldman Sachs research described as replacement of the equivalent of 300 million full-time jobs globally. It also reports the August 2025 version of Stanford's 'Canaries in the Coal Mine?' paper: a 13% relative employment decline among US workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations since widespread generative-AI adoption, concentrated in occupations more amenable to automation than augmentation. The guide supplies no more precise observation window or methodological detail for that result. Its Derby City Council example contrasts the council's stated augmentation aims with an FOI disclosure that two full-time-equivalent customer-management positions had been eliminated; the guide places this alongside a £7 million AI contract announced in February 2024, without furnishing a causal analysis. A Peterborough case similarly attributes administrative headcount reductions to increased technology use, particularly AI, without quantifying them. For wellbeing, UNISON cites Institute for the Future of Work research showing correlations between exposure to newer technologies and lower quality of life, and a 2025 qualitative study involving 12 focus groups and 84 participants that found mixed, context-dependent effects. These cover technology beyond AI and do not establish an AI-specific causal effect. Union seminar accounts provide examples of covert webcam capability, call-centre intensification and tracking-based performance pressure. For discrimination, the guide cites a 2025 NIHR study finding gender differences in some LLM-generated care summaries, a Data Justice Lab review for TUC Cymru, and the ICO's 2024 recruitment-tool audits. The Uber Eats facial-recognition example is a settlement following discrimination allegations, not a reported judicial determination of discrimination. Stronger regulatory case evidence includes the ICO's February 2024 enforcement against Serco Leisure and associated organisations for disproportionate biometric attendance monitoring affecting more than 2,000 employees at 38 facilities. Worker opinion polls support claims about anxiety and preferences, not realised job losses. Government and professional guidance supplies authority for accountability, security and implementation-cost concerns. Environmental examples are secondary calculations and projections rather than measurements of UNISON workplaces.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The September 2025 guide distinguishes current adoption from open-ended forecasts and makes beneficial outcomes conditional on implementation, safeguards and worker involvement.
pts.d: The central account concerns technologies already operating by September 2025, supported by research mainly from 2023–2025 but also by older surveillance cases and surveys. UNISON predicts increasing AI use throughout the public sector without setting a completion date, pointing to government reform plans, the autumn 2024 NHS technology funding pledge and August 2025 announcements of tools for the NHS and probation services. Its major productivity and job-risk figures generally have no explicit forecast deadline in the supplied text; the dates attached to reports should not be treated as deadlines for their predicted outcomes. UNISON qualifies displacement claims by saying complete job automation is relatively rare, augmentation is more common and new jobs may arise, albeit requiring different skills. It presents NHS workforce time savings as a conditional vision rather than an assured result. Risks depend on design and deployment: biased data, inappropriate targets, opaque supplier systems, excessive monitoring and inadequate training or assessment can undermine outcomes. It says employers remain responsible for decisions made using AI rather than being relieved of their legal duties. The guide supports additional employment protections through the TUC's proposed AI Bill; those provisions are proposals, not described as enacted law. Separately, it reports that changes under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 are being phased in between June 2025 and June 2026, allowing significant solely automated decisions in wider circumstances subject to safeguards. Its model agreement proposes stronger negotiated protections, including human review, preservation of pay, no reduction in job roles and paid retraining. These are template commitments requiring agreement and workplace adaptation, not descriptions of universal rights or actual outcomes. Environmental forecasts also have distinct horizons: the cited ICT emissions projection extends to 2040 and concerns ICT generally, not AI alone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: UNISON identifies differentiated effects on public-service workers, vulnerable occupational and demographic groups, service users, employers and unions.
pts.d: Workers in administration, customer management, call centres, health, social care, local government, probation, energy and utilities face changes to tasks, skills, supervision and employment security. Lower-paid, back-office, entry-level and part-time roles are described as especially exposed to automation; women, young people and Black workers are said to be overrepresented in susceptible roles. The Stanford finding concerns US early-career workers aged 22–25, whereas the cited British TUC anxiety poll identifies particularly high concern among ages 25–34; these are different populations and measures. Disabled applicants and workers may be disadvantaged by video assessment, narrow hiring criteria or targets that ignore reasonable adjustments; employment gaps related to maternity or disability can also become a source of bias. Facial, voice and language analysis may disadvantage racialised groups, particular accents and dialects. Women aged 35–49 are identified as especially affected in the cited technology-exposure and quality-of-life correlation. Home and hybrid workers face expanded monitoring of domestic spaces and blurred working-time boundaries; community and care workers face tracking, personal-device costs and privacy risks. Call-centre staff may lose routine work but retain more emotionally demanding cases. Service users, including patients and vulnerable people receiving social care or benefits, face both possible improvements and risks from biased assessments, fabricated information, inappropriate resource allocation or disclosure of sensitive data. Employers face procurement and maintenance costs, compliance exposure, damaged trust and possible retention or productivity problems. Unions face information asymmetries and potential monitoring of union activity, but UNISON also sees technology disputes and collective agreements as opportunities for organising, recruitment and stronger bargaining. The guide predicts growing demand for technical competence alongside empathy, creativity, complex problem-solving and adaptability, and argues that workers should receive paid retraining and a share of productivity gains rather than simply bear the costs of change.
